title: Ionic bonding
examples: What is the difference between ionic and covalent bonds?
How do you know if a bond is ionic?
Can you show me an example of electron transfer?

explain.say: Ionic bonding happens when electrons are completely transferred. This usually happens between a metal and a nonmetal.
We use dot-and-cross diagrams to show this electron transfer clearly. The metal usually loses electrons, and the nonmetal gains them.
Consider the formation of magnesium oxide. Magnesium loses two electrons, and oxygen gains those two electrons.
Because the charges are held by strong attraction, ions arrange themselves in a giant crystal structure. This is called a lattice.
In a lattice, all the ions are held in fixed positions by strong forces. This makes them very hard to melt.
Think about table salt. When you break it, you are breaking the strong ionic bonds in the crystal lattice.

faq.q: What is the difference between ionic and covalent bonds?
faq.a: Ionic bonds involve the complete transfer of electrons between atoms. Covalent bonds involve the sharing of electrons between atoms.
asks: Do electrons have to be shared?
What is the difference between sharing and transferring?

faq.q: Do all compounds have ionic bonds?
faq.a: No, some compounds form covalent bonds instead. The type of bond depends on the elements involved.
asks: Can I mix metals and nonmetals and get only covalent bonds?
When is a bond definitely not ionic?

faq.q: Why do metals tend to lose electrons?
faq.a: Metals have low electronegativity, meaning they easily give up their outer shell electrons. This forms positive ions called cations.
asks: What makes metals give away electrons?
Why are metals good at forming positive ions?

faq.q: What is the structure of an ionic compound?
faq.a: Ionic compounds do not form individual molecules. Instead, they form giant crystal lattices where positive and negative ions alternate.
asks: What is the shape of an ionic solid?

faq.q: How do I draw the dot-and-cross diagram correctly?
faq.a: Remember to show the electron being transferred fully from the metal to the nonmetal. The metal side should look like it has lost electrons.
asks: Where do I put the dots for the lost electron?
Should I cross out the electron after transfer?

facts: Ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal.
The transfer of electrons creates oppositely charged ions.
These ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces.
Ionic compounds exist as giant crystal lattices, not discrete molecules.

quiz.say: Which process describes the formation of an ionic bond?
quiz.why: This transfer creates the necessary positive and negative ions for the bond.

wrong.1: Sharing electrons describes covalent bonding, not ionic bonding.
wrong.2: The attraction must be between oppositely charged ions.
wrong.3: This is a concept used for describing covalent bonds.

quiz.say: If sodium forms a cation, what does this mean about its electrons?

options.show: It has lost one or more electrons
options.say: It has lost one or more electrons

quiz.why: Losing electrons gives the atom a positive charge, forming a cation.

wrong.0: Gaining electrons results in a negative ion, an anion.
wrong.1: Bonding requires a change in the electron count.
wrong.2: Sharing describes a different type of chemical bond.

quiz.say: What is the structure of a solid like potassium chloride?
quiz.why: The strong attraction keeps all ions fixed in a repeating crystal structure.

wrong.0: Most ionic compounds are solids with high melting points.
wrong.1: The strong lattice forces resist easy flow.
wrong.3: Ionic compounds are not small, countable molecules like water.
